title: Weather and small talk
goal: Filling the silence — weather, food, traffic jams, and the small talk that opens the door to every friendship in Malaysia.
bekal: talking about the weather with the expressions Malaysians actually use
opening and closing small talk with someone you've just met

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Waiting for the rain to stop
dialogs.intro: Wednesday afternoon. A sudden downpour traps Sarah under the roof of a bus stop with an older lady who is also waiting.

notes: **Musim tengkujuh** is the northeast monsoon season that hits the east coast of Peninsular Malaysia from around November to March. The word appears in every Malaysian weather forecast. For ordinary rainy weather people say *musim hujan* (rainy season).
**Panas terik** = scorching hot. A fixed phrase. Its cousins: **hujan lebat** (heavy rain), **angin kencang** (strong wind), **cuaca mendung** (overcast weather).
**Reda** = to ease off, stop (of rain). *Dah reda* = it's eased off. This is the standard word for rain stopping.
**Tak sempat-sempat** — the word is repeated to stress that something never happens even though you want it to: "I just never get round to it."

**Berbual** = to chat ⚠️. *Terima kasih berbual* = "thanks for the chat". It comes up at the end of every friendly conversation. (In Indonesian *membual* means to tell tall tales — don't mix them up.)

grammars.title: Weather
body: Malaysia has only two seasons — hot and rainy — so the vocabulary is small and quick to master. Just watch a few special words.
after: ⚠️ **Jerebu** = **haze** — the yearly smoke from forest fires that blankets Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia. It's in the news every dry season. The official term: *Indeks Pencemar Udara (IPU)*, the Air Pollutant Index.
⚠️ **Sejuk** = cold, of anything at all — a fridge is a *peti sejuk* ("cold box"), air conditioning is *penghawa dingin*, and cold weather is *sejuk*. (In Indonesian *sejuk* means pleasantly cool.)

sections.title: Starting a conversation with a stranger

blocks.text: Malaysians open a conversation with a few topics that are practically always safe, in an almost fixed order:

head: Topic
Sample opener
Why it's safe
rows: It's a greeting, not a question.
A shared complaint brings people together.
Malaysia is a country of migrants; this is normal.

blocks.text: **Dah makan?** ("Eaten yet?") needs its own explanation. It's a **greeting**, not an invitation and not a real question — like "how are you?". Just answer *Dah* (yes) or *Belum lagi* (not yet). If you answer *belum* in someone's home, though, it becomes a real question and food will appear.

blocks.title: Topics to handle with care
items: ⚠️ **Religion, race and politics** — three topics that are especially sensitive in Malaysia, above all between people who don't know each other yet. Not taboo, but not conversation openers.

⚠️ **Comparing Malaysia with your own country** — be careful. A comparison meant as praise can easily sound like a put-down, and vice versa. If you want to compare, stick to small things: weather, prices, food.

⚠️ **Nicknames for nationalities** — for example *Indon* for Indonesians, which many Indonesians find demeaning. Use the full name: *orang Indonesia*, *orang Amerika*. Most Malaysians mean no harm and will happily switch.
✅ **Always safe**: food, weather, roads, prices, dramas and songs, football.

blocks.text: **Yeke?** (from *ya ke?*) is the most common cry of surprise — like "really?" or "no way?". It's short and rises at the end. Together with *betul ke?* and *ish!*, it covers almost every surprised reaction in Malaysian conversation.
**Berjaya** = to succeed. *Semoga berjaya* ("may you succeed", good luck) appears on every Malaysian card, poster and message wishing someone well.

blocks.title: Wishes for special occasions
items: **Selamat Hari Raya** — Happy Eid. The reply: *Selamat Hari Raya juga* (Happy Eid to you too).
**Maaf zahir dan batin** — Forgive me, outwardly and inwardly. ⚠️ *Zahir*, not *lahir*.
**Selamat maju jaya** — Wishing you continued success.
**Selamat pengantin baru** — Congratulations on your wedding.

blocks.text: **Tahniah** means **congratulations** on an achievement (passing an exam, winning, a promotion, getting married). Malay keeps *selamat* (for greetings and wishes: *selamat pagi*, *selamat jalan*) apart from *tahniah* (for congratulating). Using *tahniah* correctly shows straight away that you know what you're doing.
